review:
The list of settler/Anno-like games has grown really REALLY long in the past decade, and I have been disappointed more times than I can count, with each of them being just as boring and unfulfilling as the last. 

I almost cant believe it, but this one is actually good.. like.. really good. 

The economic simulation is fully phyiscalized and works at a huge scale. No teleporting goods or people. Everything is tracked and flows seamlessly. When your hunter kills a deer, they go and actually pick that deer up and bring it home in their inventory. They then turn the deer into meat, hides, and tallow, and each unit is then physically represented as its carried off to the smokehouse or storage. The smoked meat is then picked up by the grocers and sold throughout the city. The meat eventually ends up in the inventories of various households throughout the town and when people go to work in the morning they will pick up the smoked meat and carry it around in their inventory until they are hungry and eat it. This all happens in the context of a city with hundreds of people juggling dozens and dozens of goods and materials. All this is happening under the hood, and it never lags or breaks. 

If you like city builders or econ sims, this is the one to get.

TLDR: Enormous potential to be a huge time-sink, but still needs work.

The good:
- It's a clone of Banished+Colonial Charter mod, in the best of ways.
- The graphics, music, and ambience are generally very good.
- The gameplay loop is addictive.
- The additions of combat, soil composition, crop selection, all extra dimensions to the Banished formula and force you to consider your town's layout.
- The UI is pretty good, though not perfect.
- Road building is really easy/practical!

The bad (keep in mind it's still in Early Access)
- The "tech tree" doesn't make much sense as it is right now. As other posters pointed out, you often need building A so you can have building B, but building A will be useless for a while. Then you get attacked, and need weapons, but you need iron, but have no means to make it.
- It's hard to tell buildings apart in the UI. I rely on hovering over them, because they look too similar, and it disrupts the flow.
- Really needs a tutorial. I've played a lot of Banished so I immediately knew what to do, but other users won't.
- The terrain-flatten tool is a must but it's not working. I expect that to be fixed soonish.

Best-in-class city sim management game. I'm city game obsessive, from the days of Sim City 2000 to Cities Skylines and Manor Lords, I try them all and stick with the best ones. Farthest Frontier brings the goods. It's highly engaging, challenges you with raiders and wildlife as you develop your new city. The customization is excellent, from screen resolutions to UI scaling and optimization sliders to help the game perform best on your system. I LOVE UI scaling because it allows you to play on a TV from a few feet away. The game runs pretty smoothly at 5x speed on an RTX 4080 Super at 1080p, but definitely gets bogged down once you reach ~500 people or are on a large map with a few hundred citizens. I tend to play new cities rather than enduring at Tier IV so this hasn't been a huge problem, but it's worth noting. I also wish the game had a 12x speed like Manor Lords because I prefer to speed build cities and try different scenarios to see what works best and even at 5x, progress can be a little slow at times.

Raiders are my favorite part of this game. They scale up based on the size of your city, starting with 4-6 raiders causing trouble up to 100+ raiders with barricade busting forces laying waste to homes, markets and storage areas. I have played with raiders and wildlife set to maximum aggression because it keeps the game interesting between build outs. The looming threats force you to be mindful of city size and grid development, ensuring optimal routes are the focus of the game to avoid losing villagers.

In early access, the game was easier to play as a beginner because the upgrade tree was based on the base command center level (e.g., unlock specific buildings at Tier II, Tier III etc.) Shortly before launch, they added a tech tree which is massive and not super well organized. The UI scaling also doesn't seem to apply to the tech tree so you need to play at a lower resolution (1080p) on a 4K display in order to see what the different options are without squinting (again, from a few feet away.) I appreicate Manor Lords for their grouping of tech tree components. That all said, I have adapted to the tech tree and they have done a nice job of making it a choose-your-adventure style gameplay by allowing you to put knowledge points into what matters most to you, like mining over defenses. Once you have ~40 points in the tech tree, it becomes considerably harder to earn knowledge so you have to choose carefully because overinvesting in other areas can lead to a less fulfilling end game because knowledge point development speed ups were not prioritized early enough.

Improvements could be made to the way resources are populated on the map. If you choose a Medium size map, the resources are all much closer together and then quite spread out if you choose a Large map. It would be better (IMO) to keep the resource density of the Medium maps and just increase the amount of resources on the Large map. You have to travel great distances and it can take forever even on cobble road so it makes the Large map less enjoyable as a whole when resources are few and far between. Additionally, the game REQUIRES clay to develop the school, healer's house and other key game achievements to keep progressing. Unfortunately, there is no guarantee that clay will be on the map, so it forces you to add a Trading Post sooner in order to develop those buildings. I suspect this is due to some older decisions, when a Tier II Command Center made mining for clay and sand available. This is no longer default, and you have to unlock mining in the tech tree, even if you get the Tier II Command Center. This hiccup causes pain in the early development of your city and I can appreciate that clay may not appear on every map, but sand does and if one does, why not the other? Especially since you don't actually NEED sand to develop infrastructure in the same way that you do clay.

There are some UI issues that I experienced at 1920 x 1080, namely the confirmation screen (e.g., Do you want to delete this?) is off-screen and impossible to bring back into the game window. There was also some initial confusion around how to manage policies. I can access them by using the 'J' hotkey but outside of that, how do I access policies? It was very confusing until I figured out the right key to press and I don't see an on-screen element to click that brings up the policies screen.

In conclusion, I think you have to be someone who enjoys challenges if you want to excel at this game and I am, so I do. :) There is a "Pacifist Mode" that removes raiders and it took away the most enjoyable change agent in the game so I don't use it, but it may be of interest to others. You still have to survive so it's not exactly a sandbox free-for-all if you choose that mode.

I also want to commend the developers on an incredible feat. I have played Banished, Manor Lords, Town to City, Foundation, Cities Skylines I & II, all the Sim Cities, Two Point Hospital, Tropico etc. This game is the best out of all of them, by far. Farthest Frontier lets you get into the nitty gritty and manage hundreds of citizens at scale. It is glorious and pretty well balanced. I wish there were more decoration options, but you can build a nice city/base with the handful of existing options. Highly recommended, it's the best city builder of 2025, hands down.

I was initially apprehensive, but I took a $25 bet and it paid off in a big way. 

Farthest Frontier is very much a spiritual successor to Banished. It’s a medieval town-building game where your primary antagonist is nature and entropy. However, where a game of Banished always felt like min/maxing a map, FF allows for more creative freedom in designing your town. Plus, it looks better. Also, plus it’s honestly just more fun.

There are negative reviews pointing out that it doesn’t share a level of complexity with something like Cities: Skylines, where you need to micromanage every aspect and that’s true. It’s more meditative. More chill. FF isn’t without challenge, but it’s a low level of challenge that affords you the time to be creative. 

I’m always looking for the right mix of 4x and The Sims and so far, this game is scratching that itch.
Great game if you are interested in travelling time. You will start playing at a given point in time and end your session at 5am a few days later and remember you forgot to eat.

As a decades+ player of Age of Empires, and thirsty for a game that focused more on building and development over combat and seeking conquest-dependent game completion, I could not have jumped higher at the chance to test this game out. My first impression was very positive. It's immersive with incredible attention to detail. A few things I don't like: as a casual player, I would have liked an easier 'easy mode.' I found the learning curve a bit steep and a possible deterrent to players unsure if they would enjoy a game like this. There is so much to do and so much to keep track of that, while wonderfully realistic, can make it seem more like a job than a game, just keeping your villagers alive. One suggestion for improving this that I would like to strongly emphasize over any other is to make hunting and fishing more influential sources food. Right now, all maps seem heavily dependent on your farming capacity, but maps like lakes limit this, but the restrictions on fishing prevents that from being a viable replacement, which seems to be the point of the map. Making hunting and fishing nodes more influential would also help offer players more options in what kind of settlement to build, noting that these nodes still require a fair bit of space to be usable (ie. I don't think this adjustment would be unbalanced, as you cannot build on water or too close to hunting spots. Second importance is waste. I would very much like to be able to assign waste collectors to designated locations, much like rat trappers, if only to help with the issue of waste collectors being idle or working the same area while waste is accumulating somewhere (else). Other quality of life improvements might be things like limiting immigration and birth rates more when supplies are low, not just when villagers are unhappy, dedicating villagers to gather or build instead of varying degrees of either, and making priority setting more influential (I once had a farm set on priority and it still took 5 years before it got built!)

Overall I'm still enjoying the game quite a bit, and look forward to the full release!

The biggest problem with Farthest Frontier isn't balance, difficulty, or complexity. It's that the game constantly wastes the player's time.

This is one of the most beautiful and immersive city builders on the market, which makes its quality-of-life problems even more frustrating because they're not hidden behind a bad game. There is an excellent city builder underneath all of this, but interacting with it often feels like fighting the interface instead of managing a settlement.

Take building site management. If I place twenty construction sites to test a neighborhood layout and later decide it doesn't work for what I'm trying to build, I can't simply drag-select them and press Delete. I can't bulk-cancel them. I can't use the so-called "Manage Buildings" tool. Instead, I have to click each individual build site, move my mouse across the screen to the delete button, click it, move my mouse back across the screen to confirm, and repeat that process for every single structure. Twenty build sites means roughly sixty clicks for something that should take seconds. What's even more baffling is that the "Manage Buildings" tool doesn't actually manage buildings. It manages roads, plazas, decorations, walls, towers, and shelters while excluding one of the most common things players actually need to manage: building sites.

That design philosophy shows up everywhere. The game constantly pushes the player through extra menus and unnecessary steps for routine actions. Want to remove construction plans? Open a window. Want to review or manage large groups of structures efficiently? Good luck. Many systems feel designed around repetitive manual interaction rather than giving the player practical tools to manage a growing settlement. The larger your town becomes, the more obvious these shortcomings become.

This lack of clarity extends into one of the most frustrating parts of the entire experience: logistics and system transparency. The game often provides minimal feedback about why production chains are failing or stalling. You’ll see messages like “production halted” or notice critical shortages without clear explanations of what caused them or how to resolve them efficiently. Resources appear to exist in the settlement, yet aren’t being delivered where they are needed. Workers behave in ways that are difficult to predict or diagnose, and instead of clear diagnostic tools, the player is left to manually trace problems across multiple buildings and storage points. In a city builder where logistics are the backbone of progression, this lack of visibility turns problem-solving into guesswork far more often than it should.

This leads into one of the game's biggest recurring issues: many systems don't behave the way players would reasonably expect them to. The flattening tool frequently behaves more like a smoothing tool than a flattening tool. The Manage Buildings tool doesn't actually manage many of the structures players most commonly need to manage. Expensive hedge fences and iron-wrought fences provide no desirability despite being some of the most visually appealing structures players can build. Time and time again, the game teaches players that the obvious solution is not the correct one. Instead of feeling intuitive, many systems feel like they require players to discover workarounds for problems that should not exist in the first place.

The desirability system is perhaps the clearest example of this disconnect. Hedge fences and iron-wrought fences are some of the nicest-looking structures in the game. They're expensive, visually appealing, and exactly the kind of thing players naturally want to use when creating attractive residential districts. Yet they provide absolutely no desirability. Their practical purpose is largely limited to controlling animal access, while a handful of cheap gardens provide significantly more value for improving residential areas.

The issue goes beyond fences. Many structures that clearly exist to improve the appearance of a settlement contribute nothing to desirability at all. Every aesthetic investment should provide at least some benefit to desirability, even if it's small. The amount can scale based on cost, prestige, or upgrade level, but when players spend resources making their city look better only to discover the game doesn't recognize that effort, the system feels arbitrary rather than intuitive. A small garden should not outperform nearly every other beautification option simply because it happens to be one of the few objects the system rewards. The game should encourage creative city design, not funnel players toward a handful of mathematically optimal decorations.

Ironically, the desirability system also exposes another problem with the terrain system. The flattening tool frequently requires multiple passes and often struggles to create suitable construction space without creating awkward-looking terrain. In practice, I've found that decorations and gardens do a better job preparing building areas than the dedicated terrain tools. By placing inexpensive decorative objects across an area, I can preserve the natural rolling hills, create flatter building footprints, and prevent structures from clipping into terrain more effectively than if I had used the actual flattening tool. When decorative objects perform the job better than the system specifically designed for that purpose, something has gone wrong at a fundamental level.

One recurring theme throughout Farthest Frontier is that players are often rewarded for finding workarounds rather than engaging with the systems as intended. The most effective solution frequently isn't the tool designed for the job, but some unrelated mechanic that happens to produce a better result. Gardens become superior desirability generators compared to more expensive beautification projects. Decorative objects become better terrain preparation tools than the flattening system itself. Rather than reinforcing the game's mechanics, these situations encourage players to bypass them.

What makes these issues especially frustrating is that they all point toward the same underlying problem: a lack of focus on player interaction and quality-of-life in a genre built around managing things at scale. Many actions still require repetitive one-by-one interaction long after the settlement has grown beyond the point where that makes sense.

What makes all of this so frustrating is that none of these complaints are about wanting the game to be easier. Good quality-of-life features don't remove challenge; they remove unnecessary friction. They respect the player's time and allow the player to focus on meaningful decisions. Farthest Frontier often does the opposite. Too many systems feel like they were designed around workarounds rather than convenience, forcing players to spend time wrestling with interfaces instead of building cities.

The tragedy is that beneath all of these issues is arguably one of the best city builders in the genre. The atmosphere is fantastic, the visuals are fantastic, and the core simulation is genuinely compelling. But after years of development, it is difficult to understand why so many basic quality-of-life problems remain unaddressed when they affect some of the most common actions players perform. Farthest Frontier doesn't need more content nearly as much as it needs the developers to modernize the experience, embrace intuitive design, and start respecting the player's time.

I thought this game was pretty good until they added raider camps. Completely pointless addition that added nothing more than a new way for your village to go into a death spiral early to mid-game. 

  Hunter AI will try to attack them on sight for some horrible reason, and sprint into their towers range and die. A new hunter will be assigned, and laborers will try to recover the previous hunters corpse. They enter the towers range, and die too. More corpses means more laborers try to recover more bodies. You cannot stop them from doing so, only temporarily interrupt them by giving them orders to stand around and do nothing, and when that order expires they will continue to try and recover corpses. 

  This has happened to me twice on different seeds, with my only solution being to completely restart. There is no way to turn these camps off besides Pacifist Mode, which turns all threats off entirely. On my third restart, I had the misfortune of having ANOTHER goddamn camp spawning outside my range of vision, only discovering it when a hunter wandered into its radius again. This time however, I didn't make a graveyard, so my villagers wouldn't try to recover bodies. This meant though that any time a villager died in my village, it would cause plague to spread due to the corpses being kept in houses.

  It's incredible how a single shitty addition manages to completely brick the game. Everything else about the game I love, but why in god's name would you ever add a feature that amounts to "Villagers die if they enter this area", and provide no means of keeping them out of the fucking area? There isn't even any reward for killing raider camps besides "delaying" future raids. It's made it genuinely unplayable.

  Either remove these stupid fucking camps, give us a way to tell villagers to avoid them, or make it so Hunters dont try to 1vX the entire camp. Or just give us a way to turn them off.

I read the negative reviews, for a while they kept me from buying the game, and now I see most of the complaints are nonsense. 

Food decay isn't a real issue unless you plan poorly. Tons of ways to make food (foraging, hunting, fishing, farming, fruit trees,  ranching, trade). Grain, preserves, cheese have very slow decay. Hunting and fishing produces in winter, foraging through the other 3 seasons, and the farming and ranching can generate massive excesses as long as you have somewhere to store it all.

Trade is somewhat overpowered as you'll get 2-3 merchants visiting each year, and often at the same time. At least half the years you can buy from one for cheap and sell to the other, making a profit on nothing. I rarely found the need to sell my own goods, but it can hurry things along early on or if you're upgrading a lot of buildings. Town centre upgrades are pricey in particular but only because I try to rush them to get access to better buildings.

Markets provide a lot of gold as long as you build up enough housing around them. With amenities and making your town aesthetically pleasing you should be able to fit 20-25 houses around a market. 

Town centre can hold its own against the early raids if you garrison villagers. By the time you need towers (and have actual upkeep expenses) you'll have 2-3 market areas. Be smart about placement and it doesn't have to be expensive. Raiders want to raid/steal things, so protect the buildings with goods they might go after. Keep those buildings somewhat close to each other, also helps save money with rat catchers. If possible, put towers on higher ground as they get attack bonuses then.

The building AI can be a little annoying early on, but once you get over 150-200 population you can easily afford to change some labourers to builders. The number won't go up from the 4 initial ones unless you change it yourself. Things will be built relatively quickly then, as long as it doesn't take forever to bring the materials.

I have never had 1 house get abandoned. I don't know how anyone managed that.... maybe by building a undesirable building too close? Also, it's OK to let some villagers die. It's super easy to get more as long as you consistently improve your town.

The only legitimate complaints I saw was the frame rate stutter. I run it on max with a RTX2070 and during blizzards it's noticeable, but not unplayable. Also if you play it for a few hours it starts to get bad. Just close down the game and load it up again. I got up to 520ish pop before getting bored and it's perfectly playable still.

My complaint is you can't control what the wagons do... and they don't do enough at this point. They should stock markets and big builds but I didn't see a way to do that. 

Still missing (in my opinion): bridges, boats, chickens, horses, patrols, deep mines. A lot of the "depth" (like crop rotation) is pointless and can be ignored, so it's missing depth of substance.

TLDR: Ignore the bad reviews. Game is actually easy (way easier than Banished) and most of the complaints are based on lack of skill/planning rather than bad mechanics. I'd also say it's as feature complete as many finished games of the past.

Farthest Frontier takes the best aspects of settlement games like Banished and combines them with the mechanics of "civilization" city builders like the Sierra games (Caesar 3, Pharoah, Rise of the Middle Kingdom). This game is pretty unique as you make a settlement and all of the decisions from barely surviving carry over to give you problems/benefits later on as you expand and thrive as a town. 

This game is basically Banished+ with how it starts and how its UI/mechanics work. You start with handful of settlers and assign people to tasks. Balancing travel time and harvesting basic resources just to survive. The big difference though is there is a lot more variables like food spoilage, crop weeds/rockiness/fertility, disease and aggressive animals/raiding parties. These variables are also affected by the game having different map types and a technology tree. On an more mountainous arid map it may be better to focus on hunting and rushing into a mining - preserving meat to have long term food and trading heavily in metals/rocks. On a lush plains map it may make sense to invest technology into growing forests to have wood and just overproduce food through farming and accepting that a lot of it will spoil.

After a couple of years the settlement starts to take the form of a town. It now needs a better way to keep food from spoiling, defend itself from raiders that are growing to size of small armies, ward off diseases that are actually historically accurate in how dangerous they are and make money. Like the Sierra games houses level up and generate more taxes/hold more people from getting access to resources and luxuries (this is handled through markets, not walkers). Every level requires more and more resources and ever increasing complexity. 

However, this game is more than just a combo of the two before-mentioned games as it has alot more choice and replaybility. What is particularly unique about this mid-late part of the game is that a lot of terraforming starts to happen. Resources run out, animals overhunted to extinction, land where cattle was raised becomes fertile enough for farms or is destroyed by over farming and forests begin to disappear if technology was not invented to manage it. Unlike the Sierra games or Banished there is a lot more decisions with trade-offs. Decisions made to just barely survive may become crisis later on. However, the best part of it is that this game is intuitive and “historical” play is optimal without being forced. One example is the three-field crop rotation system of having one field fallow (fed on by animals eating clover), one growing regenerate crops that still give food and one growing intensive crops (wheat, flax) on a rotation actually works and you will likely get there naturally like your ancestors did by just playing the game optimally with the mechanics available.

[b]Farthest Frontier[/b] is a survival city-builder, the team behind [i]Grim Dawn[/i]. Unlike many traditional city-builders that lean heavily on urban planning and resource loops, this one emphasizes the harsh realities of frontier survival—disease, famine, raiders, and the constant struggle against nature.

The game begins with a small group of settlers founding a village on untamed land. Wood, stone, clay, and iron are crucial. Seasons dictate crop yields, and soil fertility plays a big role in farming success. Farming is detailed, with crop rotation, soil depletion, and even blights affecting harvests. Hunting, fishing, and foraging provide short-term sustenance, but farms are key for long-term survival. Diseases like dysentery, scurvy, and plague can spread if sanitation is ignored. Wells, smokehouses, and cleanliness are vital. As your village grows, raiders will attack. Building palisades, towers, and arming villagers becomes necessary for survival.

Tier progression unlocks more advanced buildings and technologies. Trade posts connect you to traders for rare goods. Crafting chains allow production of tools, weapons, clothing, and luxury goods, creating a functioning medieval economy.

The game has a beautiful, grounded art style with lush forests, rustic villages, and seasonal changes that feel immersive. Sound design is subtle but effective: wind through the trees, livestock noises, and the tense alarms when raiders approach.

Steep learning curve—new players may lose villages to famine or disease quickly. Late-game can feel grindy, with resource chains requiring heavy micromanagement. Performance issues on very large towns (though updates have improved this). AI pathfinding and raider behavior can sometimes feel clunky.

[b]Farthest Frontier[/b] is a rich, challenging survival city-builder that rewards careful planning and punishes negligence. If you enjoyed [i]Banished[/i] but wished for deeper farming, more survival threats, and a stronger sense of progression, this is a perfect choice. However, if you prefer relaxed, sandbox-style building like [i]Anno[/i] or [i]Cities: Skylines[/i], the difficulty and micro-management may feel overwhelming.

The atmosphere, visuals, music, farming, and overall “frontier survival” fantasy are excellent. The first 20–30 hours are immersive and enjoyable.

But the game starts falling apart because of its internal design and logistics systems (after ~40 hours you will start to notice it).

The core problem is that the game tries to simulate complex physical logistics like RimWorld/Dwarf Fortress, but without giving the player proper control tools. At the same time, it lacks the clarity and reliability of Anno 1800.

Anno simplifies many systems, but they work clearly and predictably. Farthest Frontier adds friction and complexity, but too often it feels artificial instead of meaningful.

Examples:

* Goods exist in town, but houses still don’t receive them (and you can't directly control or fix it).
* Meat spoils far away while wagons sit idle.
* Temporary Shelters get filled with food, but workers barely use them (they still travel long distances back to the main city).
* Water is treated as a “resource”, but it is not distributed through markets/storage like other goods. Villagers physically walk to wells themselves — and the game barely explains this. I lost around 25% of my population to dehydration before realizing I needed wells spammed across the entire map.
* Important progression is heavily gated behind gold and trade in a game that visually presents itself as an isolated frontier survival settlement (gold income eventually becomes the main task because security and healthcare depend on it).

The biggest issue is that the game constantly punishes the player for systems they cannot properly control.

In good management games:

* either systems are abstracted and predictable (Anno),
* or they are deep but transparent and controllable (RimWorld / Dwarf Fortress).

Farthest Frontier often lands somewhere in the middle:

* complex enough to become frustrating,
* but not deep or readable enough to feel rewarding.

Instead of “solving logistics”, I often felt like I was fighting the AI and working around strange simulation behavior.

The game has amazing atmosphere, but the logistics, AI behavior, and balance feel underdesigned and inconsistent.

It's everything I wanted Banished to be.

Farthest Frontier does some pretty good stuff within the "City Builder With Natural Dangers" subgenre, but I ended up not wanting to play it anymore. My thoughts:


[h3]Good:[/h3] 
Farming system is in-depth, but the UI makes it easy to understand. You can schedule more than one planting per season, rotate crops on a 3 year cycle, and add more clay or sand to a field to get better yields for crops that prefer one or the other.

Every disease I've seen has a cause (not enough water, bad waste management, wounds from animal attacks) so they present a nice logistical challenge rather than being entirely RNG curveballs. Playing with "Maladies" on the hardest setting is fun!

These might be the smartest sim folks I've ever seen. They somehow are good at defending AND self-preservation, they always spring into action when there is work to do, and their pathing is efficient. Best of all, they only take one long break at the end of the year instead of being stricken with periodic bouts of inexplicable laziness like in Banished. 

[h3]Neutral:[/h3] 
No way to disable raiders. I like the hostile wildlife but I find the raiders annoying.

No "set it and forget it" way of collecting lumber. I miss the forester's lodge that fells and replants trees :(

[h3]Bad:[/h3] 
My biggest issue with the game: I really dislike the unlockable building Tiers. I don't want to build 25 houses and wait for my population to grow to smelt iron for tools! You're supposed to grow carefully and sustainably, but the iron tools that the villagers need are locked until the midgame. I'd much prefer a tech tree where you spend gold to unlock single buildings. I would have more fun if I could decide, "I think I'll specialize in glassware as early as possible as a trade good for this town." As it stands, it seems like every settlement I found will progress mostly identically.

I almost like the storage system, but for discreet storage areas to be fun, I'd prefer a bit more manual control. My transport wagon drivers are spending 95% of their time idle while my clay miners spend 95% of their time carrying clay to storage. Why??? I wish I could make wagon routes.

Even after leaving early access, there have been no real improvements to make the game less dull and shallow to play.

The food and farming systems are great. Very few city builders focus this much on food production. Farthest Frontier really gives you a sense of just how much of a pre-industrial population was required simply to feed everyone, and each upgrade to more sophisticated food production has a meaningful impact on which other industries you can sustain in your settlement. 

All other systems keep shooting themselves in the foot. 

Bears, Raiders and Raider camps force you to deal with the terrible combat system. They're not really challenging, just annoying to deal with. The game is trying to take inspiration from RTS with its different unit types, formations and the general controls, but doesn't have any depth, is clunky to control and doesn't make fights feel rewarding.

After the early game, most of your time is spent waiting for your population to grow with very little to do. You have enough food? Build exactly one of the next production building you have unlocked once you have the resources for it, then keep waiting. You don't have enough food? Build whichever food building you can. That's what you do from beginning to end, with a few more exciting moments along the way when you hit a major upgrade like bread or tool production. With v1.0 you get to also research technologies along the way, which is a good step toward player agency, but you can tell that the tech tree was tacked on after the initial release.

Overall the player is stuck in a passive role, waiting for migrants to arrive and babies to grow up, which leaves way too much time to watch the workers and notice how incredibly stupid they are. They will run across the entire map to collect resources from a mine instead of taking it from a nearby stockpile, and literally freeze to death on the way during winter. Buildings will stop working for no reason while the goods they produce are way below the threshold you set.
You can't get a proper overview of your population stats such as education, age, etc, and the individual people don't have any unique traits or personalities, so you can neither effectively manage your population for strategic purposes (as in games like stellaris) nor sit back and enjoy the social dynamics as in rimworld or dwarf fortress.

Many parts of the game lack explanation and useful tooltips, even to this day.

The entire UI and feel of the game lacks a certain... something. In a game like Anno, getting to build a big shiny building has oomph and feels important, and placing down rows of houses is satisfying. In Farthest Frontier, all your actions feel a bit detached from the game world, like you're clicking buttons in an old-fashioned menu.

Once you've unlocked and built all the buildings once, there is no replay value and nothing to achieve.

If you take a look at my profile you will see a staggering amount of city builder / survival games that have all tried to emulate one title, Banished. I have played thousands and thousands of hours of these kinds of titles and while I like where Farthest Frontier is going, it needs a bunch of tweaking. It has a number of good and bad mechanics, some which can be corrected I think. 

The Good:

- The graphics are fantastic

- There are outside threats that will cause you headaches a la RimWorld

The Annoying/Bad/Fixable:
Every society has used quarries and foresters to manage these resources or dig them out of a more central place.
- You need a stone quarry, Crate, or some other way of getting stone other than trading or finding rocks on the ground
- Same goes for reforestation. These are pretty critical resources that get harder and harder to collect. 
- Black smithing is way, way, WAY to far into the game to be useful. It's a late game item, but you get slaughtered by Raiders because you have nothing to defend with other than towers that shoot arrows because you cannot build the swords, armor and shields. - Never enough food in the area. Hunting is countered by expansion and in some cases, will disappear
- Foraging doesn't produce enough because eventually you are walking too far
- There is no logic to the wagons that I can decipher. Most of the time they are idle.
- Markets have 1 employee. Banished allowed up to 10. Markets are frequently out of stock making sims walk stupid distances for food, slowing their work progress
- Temporary homes are a neat idea, but need more explanation
- Markets need more explanation
- Resource logistics needs more explanation

- I hate the trading interface to stock stuff. It needs like 3 less steps.

I'm going to keep playing as they update it, and updating this. I know it is E.A. lots of time. I just expected a bit more.

It’s an okay city-builder, but it really doesn’t feel like a finished product. Steam "really" need an "okay" than just yes and no.

That’s the main reason is there is a lot of negatives, not because it’s bad, but because there are better and more complete options available right now. Most of the issues could be fixed later, but at release, it’s rough.

A lot of basic features are still missing or inconsistent. Windowed mode and “play in background” don’t work properly and sometimes just disappear from the settings menu, in a game with a lot of idle waiting, that matters. There are also no resolution settings at all, which feels bizarre in 2025.

The recent tech/upgrade rework also didn’t improve much. Most research choices fall into one of three categories:

* Pick the obvious gathering/crafting upgrade
* Avoid the pointless upgrade
* Unlock the next building that really should just have been tied to the Town Hall upgrade

There’s no real specialization, the system mostly just slows you down.

Some buildings feel like they are in the wrong tier entirely. The Healer’s Hut, for example, should be a basic early-game building (we’re talking herbal medicine here), but it’s stuck in a tier that makes early game unnecessarily punishing. On higher difficulty, one random wolf far away from its den can mean a villager bleeds out, because the healer is locked behind too many steps, no one can do anything.

The pacing is also strange. The game starts fast, then collapses into a very slow phase where gold income is weak, most buildings cost 100+ gold, and you basically wait. (Yes, you can bypass the gold problem by placing the smallest possible field just to unlock the Apiary and print honey → gold, but that feels like exploiting the design, not playing it. And you still not big enough village to make an decent production line)

Then when the production line is up and the children finaly grow up, you suddenly swim in gold and villagers, and the entire pace flips into a rush toward endgame. A lot of time feels like AFK idle, followed by instant acceleration from T2 and straight to T4.

Combat is also undercooked. You’re suggested to build walls early on, but they’re too expensive for that stage, so it’s more efficient to just rally the entire population and swarm attackers. There’s also no cheap early melee weapon like a wooden spear , you get bows early, but units still prefer melee unless they archer/hunter (you can "game this" by having a lot of hunter hunts that you fill up during an raid to get cheap non-gold archers). Metal production also comes in late in T2, which makes early defense feel clumsy and inconsistent. An "milita with spear" from the townhall where they just grab an stick would help a lot.

On harder map settings, the “challenge” often becomes staring at the trade screen more, especially when important resources like clay are missing and you end up trading honey for clay for half the game to you get out of the early production and decent production lines.

Overall:
If you push through the rough parts, it can be a decent city-builder. The atmosphere is good, the core loop is satisfying enough, and there’s potential here. But it is absolutely not finished, not well-balanced, and not well-tuned for pacing or play flow. If you’re okay with that, you may still enjoy it. If you want a polished city-builder right now, there are better choices.

I teetered on not recommending this for a good few minutes before I decided to write this review.  

For being version .80, the game is good.  Crate entertainment is a group of guys who REALLY take what they do seriously and with pride and professionalism.  As far as I can tell, they also listen to feedback from people. 

Pros:

Excellent city building/survival experience that rewards you for being efficient and thinking ahead, with decent graphics and a reasonably good UI.  

The technology/build tree is logical and makes sense, but you are definitely not handheld and spoonfed on what all to do first and when.  

Cons: 

The map can vary so much in its seed generation that you can potentially be spawned with not a single iron, gold, sand, or clay node anywhere near you, and expanding to find them is too punishing (it was for me at least).

HUGE bodies of water can run out of fish very quickly, and a lot of the time there isn't any other source of food nearby (deer spawn spots are somewhat rare for some reason it seems).  

The worker AI seems like it is very, very low intelligence sometimes.  if I have a plot planned to build a shelter and I select the harvest the nearby trees, the AI would rather walk clear across the map back to the storage and grab lumber instead of just cutting the nearby tree and bringing it back to the build spot.   Same with stone, etc.   Trees feel like they should provide a lot more lumber than they do for the time and effort it takes to cut one down and haul it back.

Wagon drivers are slower than walkers which doesn't make any sense to me. 

Your workforce can get spread so thin with just trying to keep food up that you won't have any gold/resources leftover to make sure you have a trained militia/guard towers to stop that inevitable 46 raider attack squad that comes in and just decimates your town and steals your precious gold and food. 

I'm glad they let you turn off illness/injury notifications because holy HELL, when you get a high population count it spams the crap out of you telling you about every bout of diarrhea and broken bone that happens.

Building walls around your city is a chore. I would rather it come with a set square or circle placement pattern/telegraph that you place and can increase or decrease its size to place it, or let you place eliptical guiding nodes where you can shape it around your city.  

Storage AI needs a good bit of work.  Multiple root cellars and storage buildings, but that fish shack/smoke shack STAYS full and even with wagons, nobody seems to want to come get the excess and add it to a market sometimes.

Farming...oh god the farming.  I have 5 HUGE farmlands and it's an entire game almost by itself managing all that....composting, tilling the field with workers (which should take a lot less time than it does), rotating the crops...and on top of all that, dealing with the endless flood of diseases, heat stroke, frost, animals eating your crops.    It's a nightmare.  Some things in the game, I feel need less micromanagement, like the poop/compost mechanic.  As in, the compost worker should automatically take the compost to the field with the lowest fertility rate.    SOME automation would be nice between buildings.  

Barracks solders should automatically leave the barracks and go where the raiders are, especially given the cost and time and technology required to bring them into existence.  Towers near farms should automatically shoot down animals eating your crops in the field.  Or hunters nearby should shoot them, too.


I am really enjoying the game so far, but it does need a good bit of work and polish. There is such a thing as too much micromanagement: I think the game crosses the line on that in a few areas, and then it becomes convoluted and frustrating, like you're just meant to fail because of how much is going on that your brain can't maintain it all.

My biggest settlement is 249 population, and it seems perpetually stuck at 4 months of food with 1 spoilage rate no matter what I do.  Fish need to restock faster. Deer need to respawn faster (Hell, the people in town reproduce faster than animals in the woods seem to LOL)

I rarely, if ever write reviews, but here goes.

This game is still in early access so take what I post with a grain of salt. 

To start, the game in it's current form, as of August of 2025, is a solid game in concept and it plays fairly smoothly. 

Pros:

1. It saves automatically quite often. I cannot express to you how absolutely useful and user friendly this is for gamers. Many games that should have auto save capability do not have it, and it's always a big reason why players lose interest once that first big mistake happens and they then lose hours, or sometimes an entire play through.

2. Buildings in this game can be moved instead of having to tear them down and reconstruct them. Many city builders seem to think that it is in the best interest of the game play to force players to lose resources AND time in tearing buildings down, only to then make them use more to build new ones. This is especially aggravating when it comes to upgraded buildings that require fully upgrading them over again. In FF, there is no such issue, you simply move the building to the desired location and it automatically repopulates and begins working as intended.

3. Most of the upgrading system for buildings is in a good place balance wise. There are a few notable black marks, but otherwise, the meat and potatoes of the game works well and each building upgrade seems to fit the need of the designed age or era in game play.

4. FF has multiple different map types and customizable difficulty levels that it allows you to control. The options to change your challenge levels are very in depth and provide massive replayability.

5. Upgraded buildings allow for automated resource gather for some of the most basic resources in the game once you have made it midway through a play through. This frees up time to focus on a larger city and not become overloaded. Many games do not handle this aspect well and become a slog by forcing players to endlessly pause the game just to continuously micro-manage even the most basic resources.


Cons:

1. Micro-management can become tedious at times, especially late game when your city becomes very large. Most city builders suffer from this so it is not a big surprise, and FF handles it fairly well, but it still becomes tedious nonetheless at city populations at or over 500.

2. Food resources are inconsistent in their use by villagers. The marketplace is supposed to supply dwellings with food, medicine, and basics like firewood and water. Unfortunately, I find that even with a fully upgraded marketplace and all villagers occupying it, they still cannot keep up with just 25 or so dwellings. I have witnessed behaviors where workers will take resources from one house, to another house, then back again, doing nothing but wasting time. 

3. Useless tasks added by developer. About 6 months ago, the developer, for some unknown reason decided to make workers go do things like "laundry", "sorting", and "cooking".... these actions might seem to make sense from a realism standpoint, but they only serve to take workers away from their appointed tasks. An example I recently encountered was a forager going to harvest berries, who picked about 10 berries, and abruptly dropped them to go do laundry. Then, when finished, they went to get more berries, and stopped halfway from the berries, then walked all the way back to their hut to cook. This cost over 2 months of in game time for that one worker, which represents about 25% of their entire available gathering period. All for nothing. This was not needed, and never should have been added to the game, as well as NO ONE asked for it.

4. Forager huts need to be fixed. Foragers were initially fairly useful, then were programmed to be so productive when upgraded that it made farming nearly useless. Then when they were patched to rebalance them, they were nerfed so badly that there is never a reason to have any more than 1 or 2 forager huts and NEVER to upgrade them at all. Upgraded forager huts need to be able to move any plant into their garden while simultaneously STILL being able to gather out from the wilderness. Currently, forager huts are unusable.

5. Terrain management needs to be upgraded so that we are not reliant on getting lucky just to find a plateau to place our town center on. If we can level terrain, then there is no reason we cannot raise or lower terrain. The current system requires hours of tedious point by point manipulation of terrain in order to get the desired result.


Overall, I DO recommend this game, however, I would say that it has a long way to go and the developers need to stop adding things into the game that drag villagers away from designated tasks. Realism is one thing, but functionality in games like this is far more important.

TLDR: Great game in early access. Needs more content and a few quality of life changes, but otherwise made me feel fulfilled building my medieval world. 

To the general public; its a great game in early access, Steam recommended the title after enjoying Frost Punk and I decided to give it a go. In this game you manage the survival of a medieval town that has a number of interesting environmental difficulties; crop field fertility, disease, population need/wants and predatory wild life that can kill your village. I found the crop rotation concept novel and interesting and I especially enjoyed the village economy with traders, mining activities and the production of various raw material and commodities. Overall its a really interesting and stimulating city builder / survival sentiment game. I did, however, have some distinct issues with the game. Late game lack content; after city hall level 4 there's not much to do other than optimise resource collection and I no longer felt that stimulating. Additionally, large sentiments tended to create very low frame rates (sub 10 frames per second, real power point stuff) even on my 1060 GT (6GB). I spent 30 hours in game and felt I achieved all that could be done as of the 8th of June 2023. I look forward to more content. 

To the devs: You're doing a great job, really enjoyed your game, and I feel you've created a lot of unique systems that make your game fun and interesting. Some general suggestions for the future; 
1) Please include a map. I explored a rather large area and often found myself struggling to remember resource locations which made village planning difficult. 
2) More content above town centre level 4; I feel as though at this point in development some large leap should take place, instead I was left feeling a bit underwhelmed. The town naturally leaned towards an industrial revolution at this stage where mechanisation would begin to take shape; steam powered manufacturing of goods and the beginning of foreign trade would be the natural fit for this stage of the game. Alternatively, an education enlightenment and the beginning of research into lofty subjects that could improve daily life. 
3) A friend of mine suggested incorporating religion into the game that can effect things like population mood and crop yields with random events would also be a welcomed addition. 
4) some graphics issues happened at larger towns with really poor frame rates even with my fairly equipped card for such a game. Some optimisation may be necessary to improve graphics processing.

Review:  
Farthest Frontier could have been a fantastic city builder, but the developers refuse to fix the core problems that make the game collapse long before it becomes interesting.

Instead of addressing the fundamental issues — a heavily serialized simulation loop, what's seems to be single‑threaded pathfinding, and zero real optimized multithreading — they keep adding small gimmick features that do nothing to improve gameplay or stability. The result is a game that starts lagging around 500 to 1,000 citizens and becomes outright unplayable around 3,000, no matter how powerful your hardware is.

The lack of realism doesn’t help either. A town hit by smallpox where 4/5 survive would, in reality, be immune afterwards. That’s how the disease works. In the game, the same population can somehow be repeatedly wiped out by the same virus, which makes no sense.

Defense balance is equally baffling. Towers — which should offer superior range, accuracy, and defensive power — are weaker than individual hunters and archers on foot. No matter the weapon type, a fortified elevated position should outperform a lone villager with a bow. Here, it doesn’t.

Farthest Frontier has potential, but until the developers fix the engine, parallelize the simulation, and overhaul the AI and pathfinding, the game will remain a village builder pretending to be a city builder — and failing the moment your village grows beyond a few hundred people.

[h1]The good[/h1]
[list]
[*] The attention to detail is next level. The houses and buildings will slowly grow plants/flowers in their yards after they're built, if a bear runs by your barn the cows will escape and need to be captured, and you'll sometimes notice geese flying north/south depending on the time of year. The sounds effects are subject to the doppler effect from camera movement for christs sake. You can tell hours were spent on small details that hardly anyone would notice.

[*] I thought that the desirablility mechanic for houses would be annoying, but I found it actually is a great way to encourage more interesting cities. I have hardly any intrinsic creativity in these kinds of games, and usually resort to grids of houses, but needing to fit decorations and entertainment buildings near houses led to me creating more interesting and visually appealing "neighborhoods" with hardly any grid structure. Figuring out how to fit parks and pubs alongside houses ended up being one of my favorite parts of the game.

[*] The balance is so good. Not once did I get annoyed or feel like the resource management was tedious, which is surprising given the amount of materials and sub-components in the game, and the resources you're juggling change as you progress in the game since some only unlock as you build the building to produce them. i.e. later in the game, food isnt as big of an issue, but now you have to worry about entertainment/luxury items.

[*] The progression feels great. I never felt like it was dragging or that I was simply waiting around. I very rarely went above 1x speed because there was always something to do and a new milestone was always around the corner.

[*] Personally im not very picky about music in games, so take this with a grain of salt, but I find it fits the game very well and provides a nice atmosphere.

[*] As someone who rather unfairly judges games by their graphics, this game is beautiful

[/list]

[h1]The not so good[/h1]
[list]
[*] I desperately want there to be more tiers of buildings/town center, although this game is early access and the devs seem very active so im sure this will change in the future. Even as it is I think it is well worth the price, and will only get better

[*] With the defualt settings, the random events are kinda meh. Fires are a total non-issue from the beginning, sickness is too easy to deal with (I never have more than two people sick with 250+ pop and I rarely have to enable my one healers house), and dealing with raids is too expensive both in labor and gold to have a outposts and barracks staffed year-round for something that happens once every few years (in the early game, at least) A warning with time before a raid that gives you time for guards to get weapons would be an easy fix.
[/list]

I absolutely cannot wait to see where this game goes, because even in early access, this is the best game in the genre and one of my favorite games of all time.

Its a great fantasy city builder, and probably one of the best I've seen out there. Visually the game looks great and the trading system feel engaging through the whole gameplay. Its a rare survival city builder where you can make a city that's trying to survive and also have the ability to make it visually pleasant along the way.

What it does well:

- Visuals are very pretty and change through the seasons
- Gridless cities and a diverse enough selection of decorations means that you can actually make some very nice looking areas in your city if you decide to.
- Large tech tree to explore and unlock
- Resources are diverse in what you can produce/harvest/consume.
- Having defensive structures with controllable army units is cool
- Crop rotation farming system with a weather/fertility/weed/rockiness aspect of your fields which influences what you can plant and when.
- All growable resources (trees, plants, animals) have different areas on the map that are better for growing them on. So you have to take that into consideration as well as space.
- Trading is necessary, and feels more like some system for you to sell to and generate gold. On every map but the starting one, you will be usually missing something.
- Food spoiling system, foods have different storage lifetimes
- Rather than telling your total food count, it tells you how many months of food you have (as well as how much is spoiling in a year). Gives you a better idea of how much runway you have left.

What it does meh:
- City builders typically have some education mechanic in this game. It feels pretty barebones in this game and is mostly there to check a box. Would have loved if it explored it more.
- You can have town policies, and the general idea is you get some benefit but with a negative tradeoff. However, they typically punish happiness which can affect "productivity to fertility and effectiveness in combat". The policies only seem there as a "Break glass in case of emergency" button. Example: People eat less, but take a large happiness hit. I don't think I've ever had to click the buttons.
- Raiders are a bit dumb, so the fights can be fairly easy. I wish that they were more intelligent (or at least not walk in a single file line on a road if they can avoid it) It makes defensive structures questionable as by the time you can afford them, you can afford to equip enough soldiers to scare off raiders. Defensive structures feel more aesthetic than anything
- Game has a soft cap of 500 villagers before warning you that increasing it further can cause issues. You can raise the cap. I got to 650 villagers before I started a new one, and didn't notice any issues at all with my specs. Just a warning.

Bad:
- I would never recommend this to someone who is not familiar with city builders before. While the tutorial gives you some guidelines on what to do, it doesn't do a great job of helping a new player navigate the menus to find the building it wants you to build. Players who are familiar with the genre will probably do fine, but the tutorial could still use some work. Timberborn isn't as complex, and their tutorial highlights what buttons to press and where I believe, which makes it easier for newer players.
- When opening a menu for the first time (such as farming), they just info dump on you how to use the system. Its all informative and good, but you have to be fine with reading it.
- Map icons start off really small (you can enlarge them in settings). Its hard to find the resources you want on the map you've explored. They've hidden the menu to highlight resources under some buttons, but even after you find it you can only highlight the main ones. You can't highlight all the different harvestable resources on the map which can be annoying when you're trying to find good spots for your gatherers.

V0.8

Big problems:
-  Performance. Loading times are abysmal, frame rate with 400+ pop cities is punishing.
-  Poor logistics in high pop cities. High volume cart transportation between storage building might help.
-  Some mechanics don't matter - like blizzard or blight.
-  Defense against raiders is a cool concept, but current implementation is boring. Unleash this potential by encouraging player to build defenses.

Minor problems:
- Some mechanics are unclear. Basic tools, builders. Roads are mostly irrevelant inside residential areas.
- Trade automation is missing.
- Families and households not modelled.
- Desirability buildings don't show their effective range once built.

Good stuff:
- Graphics
- Food management is tricky

Overall:
Game has potential. Most of the problems can be addressed.
There are better Banished clones mechanics-wise, like Settlement Survivor, Timberborn. But this is one has it's own merits.

I've been waiting a long time for a game to replace Banished in the medieval city/survival sim genre, this is the one. It blends a lot of the strategy games into one, from Anno to AoE and it's well worth the full price.

Things fixed: they added more large resource nodes for late game. Added a better alert for when the trader shows up at your town. Fixed some tool tips and notifications. Adjusted support costs for some mid game units and buildings. And more.

Things on the roadmap: full resource production management (filtering, max limits, min limits, etc). Late game resources such as mines and other permanent sources. More late game buildings. And more.

Game Review - Farthest Frontier

Farthest Frontier is, by far, the best city builder game I've ever played. The game boasts beautiful graphics, a user-friendly management and command system, abundant resources and craftables, and much more. The developers have truly innovated to set FF apart from other similar games, not just in terms of its medieval style, but also with its unique features.

Background:
For enthusiasts like me, FF is a classic embodiment of medieval charm. Having previously enjoyed Life Is Feudal - Forest Village, FF's city theme resonates perfectly with my tastes.

Economics:
FF introduces a distinctive economy system where taxes (Gold bars) are generated from households and collected through nearby marketplaces. While the concept is intriguing, there's currently a lack of methods to generate positive monthly gains. Hopefully, the developers can enhance this aspect.

Crop Rotations:
FF stands out as the only city builder game I've encountered that incorporates crop rotation. Different crops possess unique characteristics like growth time, heat/frost tolerance, impact on fertility, and more. Farmlands also have fertility levels, weed features, and occasional disease events that significantly affect crop yields. Planning careful crop management is both engaging and realistic.

Natural Resources:
Despite the initial overwhelming variety of resources, they add depth and uniqueness to the gameplay, enhancing the overall experience.

Combat System:
For those seeking combat within a city builder game, FF delivers. Similar to Dawn of Man, occasional raider events occur. However, FF takes a different approach by having raiders prioritize looting gold and other valuable items, fleeing once they've plundered a building. This adds a realistic but more aggravating element compared to DoM.

Suggestions for Improvement:

Seasonal Impact on Professions:
Professions like foragers, farmers, and arborists remain idle during winter. Implementing an automatic labor assignment during this period would alleviate the need for constant manual intervention.

Temporary Shelter for Distance Workers:
Expanding the use of temporary shelters to include miners and foragers, not just work camp laborers, would improve overall efficiency, especially for resources located far from the main city.

Diversifying Positive Cash Flow Methods:
While luxuries generate additional taxes, the market remains the primary income source. Introducing new buildings that generate self-sustaining income (such as pubs, libraries, pastry-makers, and jewelry shops) would add depth to economic gameplay. Spiritual buildings could collect tithe taxes instead of incurring service costs.

Managing Monthly Expenses:
Spiritual buildings shouldn't impose monthly costs. Balancing the expenses associated with city facilities, particularly guards and soldiers, would create a more coherent economic model. The current cost structure for guards and soldiers should be clarified.

Productivity of Soldiers and Guards:
Adding the ability to choose how much time militia spends on guarding positions while still participating in labor work would enhance strategic flexibility. When the city alarm sounds, militia should promptly return to their positions to defend against intruders.

Curved Wall Construction:
Expanding wall construction options to include curved designs (similar to roads) would facilitate more intricate and creative city layouts.

Desirable Additional Features:

Gem Mine:
Introducing gem mines within mountain biomes that can be harvested by miners for jewelry production would add a layer of resource diversity.

Herbalist hut:
Adding a new building that allows the cultivation of herbs and medical roots.

Cavalry:
Implementing cavalry units that ride on horses, offering increased speed and combat effectiveness, would add strategic depth and mobility to the game.

Fort Building:
Introducing defensive forts that work in conjunction with walls, managed by soldiers, could provide advanced protection during raids. This fortified structure would offer shelter to villagers during attacks.

Raider Camps:
The emergence of raider camps around cities over time, requiring player intervention to send troops for pillaging and loot acquisition, would add a dynamic and challenging element.

Honored War System:
Expanding gameplay to include substantial battles against bandit and noble armies, with potential rewards based on player choices, would provide a grander sense of progression and narrative.

But like I said there are a few important items to consider:

- No matter the computer you have, it will show slow performance on late game and it's not somewhat bound to CPU/GPU/SSD. I've loaded the entire game from RAMdisk and it's taking 10% or less from my CPU and 30% or less from my GPU but still, it's slow once you reach 1200+ villagers. It's just really painfully slow. Freezes from time to time (no, not even talking about auto-save, I gave up on that, it's impossible), can't run smoothly anymore no matter what I do. I've tried everything including new install, GPU settings and more.

- Raiders become boring over time. It's more of the same, difference being only that they will increase in numbers. After 40+ attempts this mechanic just becomes a bit boring, actually. There's no option for you to create incursions or to raid others, or even to search and kill raiders other than waiting for them to pop-up on your city.

- Lacks an option for a more mature distribution (logistics) system. Since you can't ensure goods are moved to specific places and you can't control limits for specific goods on storage facilities, you need to rethink entirely how your city will grow as it needs to fit around those facilities, otherwise travel time will be huge.

- Forges and Blacksmith order is messed up to the latest degree. You can forge weapons but you can't forge iron yet. It's just really silly and pointless.

- You have to build the lower-tier building and update. It's silly too. You should only update pre-built constructions, but once you get there there, build the latest one, even if it's more expensive. It's silly to build hunter cabin from lower tier just to upgrade it and similar.

- The logistic of building maintenance becomes a hassle on late game for very large cities. Construction workers keep losing the battle even with plenty workers there.

- You can't grow medicinal herbs or roots and this is really silly. Makes no sense as these were there all along human history.

- You also only have cattle. No chicken, sheep or anything else. Again, silly, as those were there all along human history. They could yield different things (eg: eggs for chicken, wool and other materials).

- Some buildings (like trade centre) should definitely have more workers. This is specially important for late game on a huge city with industry all around and nothing nearby anymore.

- Traders available money don't really follow the game. It's fine for early game but for late game when you have 100K+ it makes no sense to even bother selling things for traders with 4K or less.

- That initial wagon never goes away. Never. No matter how late, it will never go away. Even if it makes no sense to exist anymore and could be recycled, you can't. It will just be there, forever.

The only painful one is the performance issue. You'll start noticing a bit of that once you get past 500 villagers, and once you get close to 800-900 it will be really visible. If you're with the 1000 villagers cap off, once you get 1200-1300+ it's painfully slow, and I really really mean it.

But with the cap you won't get past 1000 so it's quite OK. And you'll have lots of fun, really.
Therefore, I strongly recommend this game for everyone interested in a medieval-style city builder with some war but not focused on that, and with a strong take on economy, resources and such.

I've played this game for almost 350 hours and I did have some fun, so I suppose you could say I got my money's worth. However, the more I understand the game the less I like it, so it's time for a review!

First of all the game has three win conditions, which are clearly very poorly thought out and/or implemented. You can "win" this game in a very short time with very little effort while ignoring or sidestepping the overwhelming majority of the game's content. I am guessing this was a last minute addition because someone thought a game is always better with a win condition than without, but... uh. This has to be either completely reworked or just removed from the game, IMHO.

Secondly, there is the combat system, which is just incredibly, ridiculously, laughably bad. Like, almost "not even worth to try to improve it" level of bad. If you want a war game, play something else for sure. I kinda knew this going in, so I don't really hold this against the devs, I just wanted to get this out of the way so that we can focus on the things that this game was supposed to be good at: settlement building.

The game has a seemingly complex economic system with a lot of components including hunting, fishing, gathering, farming, markets, livestock, bee hives, taxes, transport wagons, mining, policies, etc, etc. The exact details of virtually every aspect of the system are very poorly documented. The game does kinda explain the basics, but there is no real in-game tutorial and the official online "guide" barely scratches the surface. There is a wiki that is obviously the work of an outsider enthusiast, not the devs, and is very, very incomplete and outdated.

Because of all this some people get the impression that the game has a steep learning curve.

What I think this game actually has is a [b]very thick smoke screen[/b] hiding the fact that there is really [b]not much substance behind all this complex facade[/b].

Sure, the farming system has fertility rates, clay/sand ratios, environmental factors, composting, diseases, etc. It is kinda hard to figure out how it EXACTLY works, but guess what: it doesn't ACTUALLY matter! If you farm, no matter how badly, you will have a ton of food.

Sure, the market generates gold in a convoluted (and I might add pretty much indefensibly out-of-thin-air) fashion that I am still not sure I fully understand, and you can bang your head against the wall trying to optimize your town based on these obscure rules, but does it really matter? Not if you trade, because guess what, if you do trade you will have more gold than you know what to do with!

Sure, you can raise chickens, goats, and cows, which again seemingly adds an interesting layer of complexity, with fodder quality, fertilizing, and I don't even know what else, but the bottom line is that, you guessed it, most of it JUST DOES NOT MATTER. If you get cows, you will have a ton of milk, meat, and leather. It's basically impossible to screw this up. You can put a lot of effort into integrating your pastures into your farming, because -- what an amazing detail! -- the cows do fertilize the land they are grazing... but why would you? It's just not worth it because it doesn't matter one bit whether you fertilize your fields!

I could go on and on, there are at least a dozen other aspects of the game that at first sight seem to add variety and challenge, but turn out to be a nothingburger.

If you read some comments online from people who had played this game for a while, you will see that there are many elements that are just dismissed from the hip as completely useless. You can brew beer and sell it from a pub, but you are probably better off if you just don't do that. You can get both goats and cows, but there is really no reason to ever get goats, you should just get cows. You can grow wheat and mill it and bake bread, but it's probably not worth the effort. Just grow rye, turn it into beer, sell the beer at the trading post, buy whatever you want. You can build walls and towers to defend against the raiders but you are probably better off if you don't. You can set up a complex mining and smithing operation to turn coal and iron ore into tools and weapons, but it's almost certainly better to just buy all that stuff.

Now, to close on a semi-positive note, the best part of the game is how it looks. You can build some pretty towns for sure. Even here the game falls a bit short of 5 stars, IMHO. First and foremost the UI for building roads is surprisingly aggravating, considering how important roads are for both the smooth functioning of the town and for its looks. Nicely curving roads are half the battle when it comes to building a nice town, and the game does NOT make it easy to lay nicely curving roads. There is a lot of room for improvement when it comes to desirability improvements/eye candy as well. For example you can build statues but all the statues look the same, so your town ends up looking like the capital of North Korea with the same dude looking back at you on every corner.

So, to summarize, this game feels like [b]a very elaborate DEMO[/b] of what COULD be done, without ACTUALLY doing most of it. There is certainly a lot of potential here; I hope the devs won't let it go to waste. [b]As it stands, my recommendation would be to wait for 2.0.[/b]
