To be honest, Crate Entertainment is the last developer I would have expected to make such a radical genre shift and move away from a tried-and-true formula to create something completely new. And yet, that’s exactly what they did. They abandoned the H&S genre and decided to create a classic survival city-builder… and yet they decided to make the task even more difficult for themselves.
If you take a look for an overview of the currently available city builders you’ll notice a pattern. Absolutely every game tries to do something which will set it apart from the competition; it might be an original setting, atypical genre mix etc.  However, here, the developers decided to do things their own way, so they simply created a medieval settlement simulator. There are no hidden or overt themes, nor anything unique. Just a simple life, its hardships, and small moments of respite and joy. It’s all very familiar and, frankly, pretty cliché.

Yet it works. 

It works because the game is a realistic survival and city-builder based on sandbox mechanics. The game impresses with its complexity and the fact that it requires (just like in real life) you to meet all needs and gather all necessary resources. If you don’t provide fruit, scurvy will set in; if there’s no fresh water, dysentery and cholera will spread; if there’s no firewood or warm clothing, they’ll freeze or fall ill. If you want wine, you’ll also need to provide bottles. There’s nothing arbitrary about it. To achieve full production, you need technology, production lines for all components, and so on. 

[b]Would I recommend it? Yes. [/b] 

This game is a fantastic survival and city-builder that will satisfy anyone who wants to design realistic cities and refuses to settle for clichés. It’s clear that the game has been well-thought-out in terms of its concept, excellently executed in terms of gameplay and mechanics, and that great care has been taken to ensure all elements work seamlessly together. Yes, it has its flaws, but in my opinion, they do not detract from the overall positive experience of this game.

✅[list]
[*] Game is visually stunning, but this effect is achieved through attention to detail and overall composition, rather than flashy graphics. Every building has been hand-modeled, which is clearly visible when zoomed in. Each building upgrade results in a more detailed model, which also perfectly reflects the city’s growth and prosperity.

[*] Soundtrack was composed by Steve Pardo and is calm and atmospheric. Main theme is designed to reflect both the era in which the game is set and the so-called hardships of everyday life. To be honest, both the melody and the tempo of the tracks are a perfect fit for this game. Soundscape is also excellent. Sounds blend seamlessly into the surroundings and the flow of events. Combined with the music, they form a cohesive whole in which no single element overpowers the others.

[*] 6 distinct biomes + advanced settings that allow players to further customize the gameplay to their preferences. Additionally, all maps are procedurally generated, so choosing a biome doesn’t mean you’ll see the same layout you might have seen in someone else’s game.

[*] Agriculture. It’s probably one of the most complex systems that I’ve seen outside of the games dedicated solely to it. You need to manage variety of factors (soil composition, fertility profile, plant diseases, three-field rotation etc.), while planning and preparing fields for sowing. System not only encourages you to plan in advance but heavily suggest that you’re not planning it for next season but for the next decade.

[*] Diverse, realistic systems and mechanisms designed to reflect production processes as accurately as possible. Building a functioning, self-sufficient economy requires a tremendous amount of effort, but it also brings great satisfaction. Core gameplay mechanics are well-designed. They keep the player engaged and evolve as the game progresses.

[*] Various diseases and conditions that must be prevented. Preventive measures depend on the nature of the problem, but they cannot be ignored because a potential outbreak could, at best, set your colony’s progress back by light-years and, at worst, destroy it completely. Incidentally, this perfectly illustrates just how valuable every pair of able-bodied hands is and how important it is to ensure the well-being of your citizens.

[*] Additional government policies that can yield significant benefits, but always involve certain trade-offs. E.g. food rationing - while this can reduce food consumption in the settlement, the average level of happiness will drop significantly.

[*] Tech tree. Not every technology is groundbreaking, but each one makes gameplay much easier and increases your settlement’s chances of survival.

[*] Combat portion is more like a tower defense. You need to plan and prepare your defenses against roving bands or local armies, but all of this takes place primarily on a logistical level.

[*] Price/length ratio is well balanced.
[/list]

😐
[list][*] Entire color palette seems to be dimmed, especially in spring and summer months. Don't get me wrong, it's perfect for winter but for the warmer seasons, I'd expect bolder, more vibrant colors.

[*] UI at first glance seems to be not particulary user-friendly, but with time you learn to appreciate its design and planning. That said, due to its overall look it might be deterrent for some.

[*] It would be nice if the game offered a few different scenarios to choose from. I know that some achievements set forth a particular goal to get them, but without exception, they all require playing on a very high. Not everyone has enough time or will to do that.[/list]

❌[list]
[*] Game lacks a proper tutorial. What was added in Update 1.1 would be sufficient for the Anno series or other casual city-building games, but it isn't enough for a survival game.

[*] Unity does not really fare well in generating larger (>2k citizens) and more complex cities but lag and/or framerate drop is entirely dependent on your rig. Some will saw it earlier, while others will be able to build massive cities. Developers tried to mitigate it but it’s one of perennial quirks of an engine and can’t really be removed. I'm just speculating here, but I suppose it would be better if the developers built their own fork of the Unity engine. Though that takes time and money so it could not be viable here.

[*] I think there’s some kind of error related to the prioritization of resource transport. 

[*] Monuments need a redesign. Out of 3, only one justifies its costs while other 2 are either mediocre or bad.

[*] Game should provide better information or visual cues regarding resource depletion. In current system, it’s far too easy to miss the moment when resource levels start to decline, so far too often the game has forced me to make snap decisions to mitigate the damage. It would be much easier if I were notified in advance when deposits were running low, rather than being forced to check the situation one by one.

[*] City walls have no ramparts so most of the time archers or crossbowmen are a waste of resource. Strangely enough, they can shoot their enemies through the locked gates. Don’t know if it’s a bug or intended behavior.

[*] We’re unable to build improved versions of the buildings from the start. We only can build basic ones and then keep upgrading them till we get desired results.

[*] We should be able to enter into a contract with a merchant for the delivery of a specified quantity of goods at a specified price.

[*] Flattening ground for future mine takes a lot of time, especially in mountainous areas. It would be better if the game allowed us to build angled or horizontal mine shafts.

[*] Only one architectonical style, typical for medieval Central Europe. 
[/list]

The Merchant Script is pure RNG nonsense.

You can go years waiting for a specific resource, only for three merchants to arrive selling the exact same useless items. Performance drops off a cliff.
The optimization in late-game is frankly pathetic. No matter how high-end your rig is, as soon as your population grows and complex chains kick in, the frame rate plummets and the simulation stutters continuously. Watching a GPU/CPU struggle to simulate basic AI pathfinding in 2026 is painful.

If you just want to mess around in the early game for a few hours, you might enjoy it. But as a deep, functional city-builder? I cannot recommend it. The foundation is there, but the execution and technical state are a disappointment.

Re-review: 1.0 Playtest

If you have played Banished, then this game is effectively Banished+, with much bigger and more diverse production chains, lovely realistic graphics, and a tacked-on warfare system. The gameplay cycle is quite familiar: Start with a handful of people, chop down trees and mine stone, use those to build shelters, a hunting lodge, and a gatherer's cabin. Then use materials from those to supply a cobbler and a tanner for shoes and coats so your people don't freeze as fast and walk faster, and a basketweaver for baskets so they can carry more stuff. And of course you need storage, and a market for centralized supply, and a well for water, and then upgrading houses requires bricks which requires clay and coal so now you need a coal mine or a charcoal kiln which needs more firewood which needs more wood. It's a lovely feedback loop where you're constantly 

There's a nice ledger showing production vs consumption for each category and product, and ability to set production and storage limits, even if the system is a bit flaky. Main missing items are a stockpile graph showing how much of a product is in storage, and no way to set limits on agricultural or mined goods short of setting a storage limit and letting the crops rot or mine storage stay at capacity. There's also no way to set local vs centralized storage, aside from setting a 'minimum' for a specific item in one storage building and waiting for laborers to carry stuff when they have time.

The animations are pretty, and you can endlessly watch villagers go about their day or chill in the park, reminiscent of Anno 1800's idling/working animations. The armor changes based on equipment, and villager dress and equipment changes based on availability and seasons. They wear baskets when carrying stuff, put on coats in winter, and so forth. 

There warfare system is very barebones and feels more like an item the developers felt they had to check off rather than an integral part of the game. It's effectively a tower defense system where raiders spawn at the least-defended side of the map and make a conga line for your gold and relic storage buildings. Your soldiers maintain formation just long enough to make contact, and then everything becomes a giant brawl. On the bright side, at least raiders try to retreat when enough of them get killed or when their health falls low enough. It also feels soulless compared to the rest of the game: there are no guards patrolling the walls, which don't have a parapet to begin with for that purpose, no roaming patrols, no real decisions or choices. 

The terraforming tool is still shockingly underdeveloped despite two years of open beta. It's just a 'level terrain' tool that averages the height of the selected squares. 

In all, this is a worthy successor to Banished + Colonial Charter.

Farthest Frontier — 46.3 h played  
Score: 7 / 10 (Recommended for colony-sim fans)

A medieval survival city-builder that marries Banished-style scarcity with Anno-grade production chains.  Clearing a forest, laying out crop rotations, and fending off raider waves feels rewarding, though late-game optimization and interface friction keep it shy of genre greatness.

WHY IT’S WORTH SETTLING  
• **Survival first, aesthetics second** — Harsh winters, crop diseases, and predator attacks make every loaf of bread feel earned; expansion is a careful dance rather than a resource spam.  
• **Deep production web** — Grain ➜ Flour ➜ Bread, Logs ➜ Planks ➜ Furniture, Iron ➜ Tools ➜ Advanced Industry—each tier slots neatly into the next, scratching the “supply-chain” itch without Anno’s complexity.  
• **Dynamic farming** — Crop rotations, soil fertility, rockiness, and weed levels mean fields are living systems; mastering clover/fallow cycles is key to population booms.  
• **Tactile visual feedback** — Log piles shrink, fence posts rot, villagers haul visibly stacked crates—small touches that sell the frontier theme.  
• **Gradual hostility ramp** — Early wolves give way to large raider parties with siege rams; investing in palisades, towers, and barracks feels meaningful, not decorative.

WHERE THE FRONTIER FRAYS  
• **UI friction** — Settlers don’t always obey work-area tweaks; toggling production limits or hunting zones requires more clicks than it should.  
• **Performance drops** — Towns over 300 villagers dip below 30 FPS on busy trade days (Core i7-11700K / RTX 3090, 1440p “High”).  
• **Repetitive raids** — Enemy AI cycles predictable paths; once you perfect wall mazes, defense becomes routine.  
• **Limited late-game goals** — After Tier 4 Town Center and full luxury chains, motivation shifts to self-imposed challenges rather than new tech tiers.  
• **Pathfinding quirks** — Ox carts occasionally jam at gates, and hunters take scenic routes unless micromanaged.

FINAL VERDICT  
If you crave a Banished-style settlement slog with deeper crop science and satisfying production chains—and you don’t mind some mid-beta rough edges—Farthest Frontier delivers a compelling frontier fantasy.  Sharpen your scythes, rotate those carrots, and be ready to pause when the raiders roll in.

I bounced off Farthest Frontier twice in the past - it just didn’t click with me. But during the 2025 Summer Sale, I decided to give it one more shot. After all, it should be right up my alley: a medieval village/city builder with survival elements. I’d been craving something like that for a while.

Well, 100 hours later, I can confidently say I’ve finally found my enjoyment with the game.

The updates the developers have added over the years - new buildings, mechanics, balance changes - have really paid off. All the small things, both new and old (but refined), come together into a surprisingly satisfying package.

The game does a great job simulating life on a medieval frontier. It’s not just about growing or harvesting food - it’s about surviving winter and braving the wilds. You might feast on foraged goods in summer and autumn, but what about surviving the cold season, and worse, spring? By then, most of what you gathered last year will have either been eaten or spoiled!

That said, the game isn't without its quirks. Some resources still feel underutilized. Before the 1.0 test update, for example, Wax - gathered from bee hives - was only used for candles. It quickly piled up in storage, with no merchant willing to buy it and no other use besides tossing it. The same goes for Tallow. If you have cows, you’ll eventually find yourself drowning in it, and since its only use is soap, it becomes another resource with little purpose beyond clutter. In this game managing manpower is essential, running more than one shop might not be possible, unless you increase population limit.

Despite these minor issues, I can’t deny how much fun I’ve had. Farthest Frontier is exactly the kind of game I’ve been looking for, and I’m excited to see what the full release brings!

Review/Dev Feedback after a 125 pop brutal difficulty:

TL;DR: Stunning graphics, solid base, Weird but fun* progression arc, lots of potential to be the best if Crate keep refining it (Trading and Combat improvements for instance). 

- *Where most games in the genre keep the progression curve relatively linear and obvious (Kingdoms Reborn for instance), Farthest Frontier throws all sorts curve balls. Tier 2 market dependence being the most interesting one. For many vital parts, resources, and weapons drift by you in the market and the market alone. At first I felt frustrated by this, and a little demotivated. Pushing through that, restarting a bunch of runs, I eventually came to grips with it, and now I've come to appreciate it as a refreshing challenge. On hardest settings, surviving and stocking your surplus until that lucky moment a trader rolls through with swords, bricks, etc, brings a tension into the game that keeps it interesting. If the devs are reading this, more depth on the market mechanic would deepen that UX. The low hanging fruits are maybe: A world map with trading partners with their own trading bias? Something to think and plan around to take some of the monotony out of how random it can feel. A way to attract more traders or traders responding to my buying patterns in interesting ways.

- Entirely up your ambition with the wall system if you currently don't have plans too. Guards on walls, curved placement, additional lateral upgrade options  etc. The combat is actually surprisingly fun, sometimes. I've had heroic hunters take a few raiders down as they approach through the woods, troops holding down a market alone but victorious, sad scenes of carts laying on the roadside, their driver slain.. Those few were a hint at the potential. With Manor Lords coming out, and Total War still very alive, people are obviously interested in nuanced combat systems in strategy/city sims. I've got 500+ hours on grim dawn, I know you guys have it in you to do something compelling with the combat and defence. It all feels more meaningful when the cabbages come in from harvest knowing I had to fight to be around for that to happen.

That's all I've got for now. Back to it! Tier 3 awaits.

Farthest Frontier began Early Access with a strong core and beautiful aesthetic, but the 1.0 release disappointingly failed to evolve beyond its "basic foundation status." The game quickly becomes dull and repetitive due to a fundamental lack of meaningful progression. The core mechanics are sound, but they do not deepen over time. Maps feel monotonous, and the raiding mechanic is less of a strategic challenge and more of an annoying disruption. Ultimately, the game offers a competent but shallow city-builder experience that gets boring quickly for veterans of the genre.

First the good:
If you are a fan of technical city builders this is a really wonderful game. There's rewarding progression from small town to city and across a complex tech tree that makes it rewarding to play. There are hard trade off decisions between people, finances and defense that make everything impactful. On top of all that, the whole game is grounded in a seasonal rhythm that will keep you coming back to play through one more year. This is a fully built game and it's pretty great as is.

The less good:
-The combat mechanics are clunky and feel unfinished. It's a very small part of the gameplay, but it could use improvement.
-It is missing a challenge, especially in the later game. It could really use another layer of difficulty (disease, refugees, severe weather, tougher raiders etc) somewhere past the halfway mark to raise the stakes.
-It could really use some more performance optimization or more levers to pull to keep the game running as the population grows.
-Since many players will be constrained on population, it could use some later game mechanics to make extraction tasks much more efficient in the later game.
-The policy tools could use more depth - I think there are 5 policies in total right now and they don't offer much in terms of risk / reward trade off.

All that to say - this game is great. It's a very fun and original take on the city builder / RTS genre.

Farthest Frontier is a functional, competent, and sufficiently enjoyable game. There's enough to like here, and while some things could've used some extra honing, ultimately there are no glaring issues in play severe enough to push me towards leaving a negative review.

But be that as it may, I found myself irreversibly drifting away upon reaching the third research tier and spending some time with it. Yesterday, I wandered off firmly intending to return the next day in order to press on. Today, I find myself deeply reluctant to continue.

At this point I'm decently convinced that I've seen and experienced enough (if not just about everything), with precious little left to extract from the game. Yes, there's a handful of buildings and production chains I'm yet to build and establish, but sticking around for their sake doesn't feel like a great idea.

[hr][/hr]
See, something's just missing in action when it comes to Farthest Frontier. Would more content help, more buildings/upgrades/technologies/resources/professions/whatnot? Would having more elaborate and tricky mechanics be of use (feels like the game's complexity "budget" was almost entirely snatched by agriculture, leaving little for all the other things)? Probably, yes, but I don't feel this'd be the full solution.

Approaching this from another angle, there isn't much happening within the world of the game, truth be told. Merchants come and go, some villagers occasionally get sick or smacked around by aggressive wildlife, raiders pop up every once in a while, random buildings erupt in flames sometimes. 

There are also blizzards, heat waves, and some crop-related complications (diseases, droughts), and the reason I'm mentioning these separately is, well, because it took me a bit of time to actually remember that they exist. That's how "big" of an impression they've left. So, basically, there are neither windfalls nor curveballs beyond an aforementioned and scarce array of unexciting options.

....alternatively, maybe I've been rewired by Against the Storm, and, moving forward, its cadence is the only one that stands a chance of doing the trick for me. I suppose I can't really exclude this possibility, can I?

[hr][/hr]
Long story short, for me it's plain as day that Farthest Frontier is an honest and solid effort, but in the end it didn't hit the spot. It certainly manages not to miss the mark completely, and for a while I was actually quite pleased with what it had going for it. 

But I was hoping it'd be a longer while, the sort of while that'd end up encompassing several separate playthroughs, not a single unfinished one.

A hesitant thumbs up at best.
